Items.Authors: James Coulson, Brent Miszalski, Simon O'Toole, Christopher Lidman, Christopher Onken, Nuria P. F. Lorente
Items.Title: Automating data reduction and archival workflows using Apache NiFi
Items.Abstract: Traditional data reduction pipelines are run on local or remote machines, that depend on user interaction for execution. This approach can lead to reproducibility and discoverability issues. Additionally, observatory sites face the challenge of facilitating secure site to site data transfer. Data Central's NiFi system aims to combine data transfer, archival workflows, and the triggering of pipeline execution to produce discoverable data products. The archive system also includes a frontend designed with a focus on user experience, with a simple permission control system to allow teams to easily control access to proprietary data. This presentation will cover the design and implementation of this system for Data Central's archive of the ANU 2.3m Telescope at Siding Spring Observatory and how we have designed our system to enable scalable data transfers, data transformation and pipeline execution for incoming observations whilst integrating archival processes and improving observability.

Items.Authors: Manuel Díaz Alfaro, David Morris, Andres Parraguez, Alexandra Tritschler
Items.Title: DKIST vent gate monitoring and exclusion pointing prediction tool for science operations
Items.Abstract: The design of the heat stop of the U.S. National Science Foundation Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope imposes pointing limitations for targets located in the off-limb corona, which vary in different directions and with time. The telescope enclosure features four sectors of vent gates that can be opened independently and whose operation depends on weather constraints. The vent gates rotate with the enclosure as the telescope tracks the sun during the day and thus their position with respect to weather may change. We present an interactive tool that displays the evolution of these variables for a particular day to help the Science Operations team monitor the use of the vent gates as well as to know when science targets in the solar corona are not observable with the telescope, increasing observing efficiency.

Items.Authors: Yoichi Tamura, Akio Taniguchi, Kotaro Iwakami, Ichiro Jikuya, Shion Takeno, Sachiko Okumura, Masaki Sakakibara, Akinobu Miyake, Masato Hagimoto, Kianhong Lee, Chihiro Imamura, Sho Fujisawa, Shutaro Inui, Masato Kato, Ryohei Kawabe, Mikio Kurita, Nozomi Okada, Juri Yamanaka
Items.Title: Millimeter-wave adaptive optics: demonstrating closed-loop correction for lowest Zernike modes
Items.Abstract: We report on a five-element prototype wavefront sensor for millimeter-wave adaptive optics (MAO), enabling closed-loop correction of tip-tilt and defocus via secondary mirror (M2) displacement. MAO is essential for large ground-based millimeter/submillimeter telescopes to maintain surface accuracy under wind and thermal distortions. Our sensor, based on radio interferometry, measures excess path lengths from the primary mirror to a focal-plane receiver. A previous two-element prototype achieved <10 μm accuracy at the Nobeyama 45-m telescope. The new five-element system, operating at 20 GHz, was installed on the same telescope. A “Moon-edge” experiment confirmed detection of wavefront gradients through strong correlation with continuum flux from the Moon. Implementing a PI controller closed the sensor-M2 loop, stably suppressing the lowest Zernike modes. This approach establishes a foundation for metrology in future large-aperture submillimeter facilities such as AtLAST/LST.

Items.Authors: Aidan Walk, Sébastien Vievard, Olivier Guyon, Yoo Jung Kim, Elsa Huby, Sylvestre Lacour, Manon Lallement, Mathias Nowak, Jehanne Sarrazin, Julien Lozi, Vincent Déo, Miles Lucas, Michael Fitzgerald, Sergio Leon-Saval, Barnaby Norris, Steph Sallum, Thayne Currie, Motohide Tamura, Takayuki Kotani
Items.Title: FIRST-PL: on-sky retrieval of Humu’s (Altair) spin axis using a photonic lantern on Subaru Telescope
Items.Abstract: The FIRST-PL instrument on the Subaru Telescope enables a new observational capability: measuring stellar spin  orientations for indirect constraints on exoplanet orbital geometry. We describe the instrument and demonstrate  data reduction techniques to measure the spin orientation of Humu (Altair), whose apparent size is over five times  smaller than the telescope diffraction limit. FIRST-PL uses a spectrally dispersed (R 3000, 630-790 nm) 19-port  photonic lantern fed by SCExAO, a dual-stage cascading extreme adaptive optics system. Using wavelength  dependent centroid shifts (i.e. spectro-astrometry) enabled by synchronous focal-plane images, we recover the  spin orientation of Humu from 100 seconds of on-sky integration. The measured position angle is −61.8◦ ± 2.8◦  and inclination angle is 44.9◦ ± 4.1◦, consistent with existing literature. This method will extend to a higher  resolution instrument targeting slower rotating stars.

Items.Authors: Timothee Tollet, Laurent Dussopt, Abdelkader Aliane, Louis Rodriguez, Vincent Revéret, Albrecht Poglitsch, Cyrille Delisle, Valérie Goudon, Hacile Kaya
Items.Title: Full-dielectric Fabry-Perot filter array for submillimeter hyperspectral imaging
Items.Abstract: For submillimeter astronomy, and for the study of the interstellar medium in particular, detection instruments must combine very high performance with compactness. In this context, we present the development of an all-dielectric Fabry-Perot filter array for submillimeter wavelengths. The spectrometer developed at CEA is a Fabry-Perot resonator composed of two Bragg mirrors formed by quarter-wave layers of microstructured silicon. These Bragg stacks provide excellent reflectivity, while the distribution of aspect ratios across the array enables spatial variation of the resonance wavelengths, in a manner similar to a Bayer array. This interference filter, simple in both design and assembly, transmits without metallic losses at cryogenic temperatures. We present here the concept, the first prototypes, and the measurements obtained at room and cryogenic temperatures, showing efficiencies above 80% and spectral resolutions exceeding 100 for a basic mirror stack (2x3 layers).

Items.Authors: Michael J. Ireland, Qianhui Chen, Joice Mathew, Shan Liu, Tony Travouillon, Olivia Andersen, Chathura Bandutunga, Taro Matsuo
Items.Title: Pyxis formation flying demonstrator updates: inter-platform metrology and precision alignment
Items.Abstract: After a brief pause, development of the Pyxis Interferometer has continued again from April 2025, with a focus on developing the technologies needed for the SEIRIOS mission. We will describe progress on creating a more robust six dimensional alignment architecture, including creating precision alignment fiducials for star-trackers and LED metrology systems in the laboratory, with a single probe beam of 50mm diameter and no starlight. Additionally, a precision laser metrology system has now been demonstrated, with micron level absolute metrology between optical paths and 10s of picometer differential metrology. This system will be essential for increasing the baseline of the interferometry beyond the few metres where LED-based metrology is sufficiently precise.

Items.Authors: Maitland Bowen, Brian Fleming, Dmitry Vorobiev, Briana Indahl, Kristina Davis, William Snyder, Kevin France, Yi Hang Valerie Wong, Alan Ochoa, Luis Rodriguez-de Marcos, Manuel Quijada, John Hennessy, Oswald Siegmund, Adrian Martin
Items.Title: The SPRITE CubeSat: science mission planning and final pre-flight integration
Items.Abstract: The Supernova remnants/Proxies for Reionization Testbed Experiment (SPRITE) is NASA’s first 12U CubeSat dedicated to astrophysics and the first orbital far-ultraviolet spectroscopic observatory with sub-arcminute imaging capability. Its science program focuses on far-UV signatures of massive stars in young galaxies, with an emphasis on the enrichment of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the escape of ionizing radiation into the intergalactic medium (IGM). SPRITE also serves as a demonstration of advanced UV spectroscopy technologies for use onboard Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) and other future space observatories. We report on the final pre-flight testing of SPRITE’s science instrument and present simulated SPRITE push-broom mapping observations of nearby galaxies and their complementary potential for future HWO observations. We also summarize the calibration and testing of the spacecraft and highlight these systems’ applicability to future missions.

Items.Authors: Rico Landman, Sebastiaan Haffert, Joseph Long, Jared Males, Matthijs Mars, Liam Koning, Laird Close, Warren Foster, Kyle Van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander Hedglen, Parker Johnson, Maggie Kautz, Jay Kueny, Jialin Li, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Jennifer Lumbres, Eden McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Lauren Schatz, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell
Items.Title: No need to modulate: on-sky results of a neural network enhanced pyramid wavefront sensor and prospects for the ELT’s
Items.Abstract: One of the main limitations of ground-based extreme adaptive optics systems (XAO) is the balance between the temporal and photon noise error. The unmodulated Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (uPWFS) promises significant gains in sensitivity over its modulated counterpart, but its practical use is limited by its linearity range. Nonlinear reconstructors provide a pathway to recover this dynamic range while preserving the sensitivity of the uPWFS, thereby reducing photon noise and improving contrast. We present the real-time implementation of a Neural Network (NN) reconstructor and show on-sky results with MagAO-X, demonstrating robust and stable correction across diverse atmospheric conditions. Furthermore, simulations of NN-enhanced uPWFS operation on future Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs) predict substantial gains for high-contrast imaging. These results validate NN-enhanced wavefront sensing as a promising, ready-to-deploy technology for next-generation high-contrast instruments.

Items.Authors: Tyler D. Groff, Hari Subedi, Evan Bray, Caleb Baker, Eduardo Bendek, Fang Shi, Alex Walter, Pin Chen, Breann Sitarski, Nicholas Siegler, Matthew Bolcar, Feng Zhao
Items.Title: Development path and verification for HabWorlds deformable mirrors
Items.Abstract: Deformable Mirrors (DMs) are the critical component for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). A baseline set of device requirements was set for a short feasibility study by some key DM vendors. Included in these requirements are previously untestable tolerances for which a verification plan must be developed. The stability requirements, in particular, are held at unprecedented temporal frequencies. Picometer-level tolerances are levied for both long term drift as well as times scales greater than 10 Hz. This work presents a shift in thinking on how to augment the DM stability requirements via power spectrum specifications, and a concept testbed that is purpose built to directly verify this. Overall, we present the combined progress on our development of the DM verification plan for HWO DM system technologies, and dive into the testbed measurements intended to demonstrate the devices are fit for exo-Earth coronagraphy.

Items.Authors: Crystal Kim, Ronald A. Lopez, W. Hawkins Clay, Joseph Redford, John I. Bailey, Benjamin A. Mazin
Items.Title: First result of order-sorting with MOMOS: Multi-Object MKID Optical Spectrometer
Items.Abstract: The concept of the echelle spectrometer that uses energy-resolving detectors is more than two decades old. Building on previous conceptual work, we present here the first ever laboratory results of spectral order sorting using a superconducting detector-based hybrid spectrometer. MOMOS (Multi-Object MKID Optical Spectrometer) is a hybrid echelle spectrometer that uses MKIDs (Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors) in the 400-800nm band. MKIDs lack read noise and dark current enabling noiseless post-observation rebinning and characterization of faint objects, as well as time-resolved photon-counting spectroscopy. With the ability to resolve energy with an R=E/dE of 7 and above, a linear MKID array takes the place of both the cross disperser and detector in the spectrometer. We have extracted the spectrum of a Tungsten blackbody source with an approximate instrument R of 600. Fully realized, MOMOS will boast multi-order extraction of five objects (fibers) with R over 3000.

Items.Authors: Celia Verdugo, Juan Cortes, Matias Radiszcz, Jorge Morgado, Kurt Plarre, Cristian Lopez, Gabriel Marinello, Andres Perez
Items.Title: Making data-driven decisions for highly efficient ALMA science operations
Items.Abstract: In 2025, ALMA achieved its most productive cycle to date, delivering 4,487 hours of successful observations, surpassing its 4,300 hour target for the first time. This milestone was partly enabled by a data science initiative designed to optimize operational efficiency through real-time analytics. We developed curated operational datasets and automated dashboards within the Dataiku platform to monitor key performance indicators such as downtime, calibration scheduling, and observation completeness. These dashboards integrate scheduling simulations, Local Sidereal Time pressure analysis, and weather forecasting, providing astronomers with actionable insights for time-critical and high-frequency observations. As a result, ALMA set a record of 137 successful hours in high-frequency bands during Cycle 11. This approach demonstrates how advanced analytics and visualization tools can transform observatory operations, enabling rapid decision-making and proactive mitigation of efficiency risks.

Items.Authors: Matt Dobbs
Items.Title: Overview of the Canadian Hydrogen Observatory and Radio Transient Detector (CHORD) project
Items.Abstract: The CHORD telescope is now being commissioned at the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory in British Columbia. CHORD provides an order of magnitude improvement in sensitivity over its predecessor, CHIME, by doubling the collecting area, increasing the bandwidth to 300-1500 MHz, and reducing the system noise to less than 50 Kelvin. Observing the sky in drift-scan mode adjacent to the wide-field CHIME instrument, CHORD provides a deep view of the radio transient sky. Its precision composite dishes provide a clean, highly redundant beam that will allow exquisite control of systematics and excellent foreground subtraction for 21cm intensity mapping. The CHORD core array consists of 512 six-meter dishes and will be complemented by two 64-dish outrigger stations located at Hat Creek and Green Bank.  I will show performance results from CHORD's first fringes with several dishes operational and present the milestones and science targets for the full CHORD project.

Items.Authors: Emaad Paracha, Philippe Voyer, Steven J. Benton, Aurelien A. Fraisse, Ajay S. Gill, John W. Hartley, Bradley Holder, William C. Jones, Lun Li, Thuy Vy T. Luu, Richard J. Massey, Jacqueline E. McCleary, Johanna M. Nagy, C. Barth Netterfield, Susan F. Redmond, Jason D. Rhodes, L. Javier Romualdez, Jürgen Schmoll, Mohamed M. Shaaban, Sayan Saha, Pablo Trujillo, Ben Boyd, Peter Bartosik, Jason Brown, Bryce Warren
Items.Title: Starlink Takes Flight - High-Bandwidth Communication for Scientific Ballooning
Items.Abstract: Scientific balloon missions have long been constrained by limited-bandwidth communications, restricting real-time telemetry, data transfer, and monitoring. In 2023, the Super Pressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) became the first scientific balloon mission to successfully integrate and utilize SpaceX's Starlink, enabling high-speed, low latency communications from the stratosphere. With Starlink, SuperBIT was able to achieve data transfer speeds ranging from 1 Mbps to over 100 Mbps, with an average file downlink speed of 16Mbps, before the Starlink antenna failed 18 days into the flight.     In this talk, we discuss the implementation and performance of Starlink on SuperBIT, detailing challenges as well as the strategies used to overcome them. We also analyze Starlink's performance at mid-latitudes, comparing it with performance seen in more recent flights. We also explore next steps towards making Starlink a standard tool for balloon-borne research, improving connectivity.

Items.Authors: Elizabeth Arcadi, Glen Douglass, Peter Tuthill, Barnaby Norris, Stephanie Rossini-Bryson, Mona El Morsy, Eckhart Spalding, Vincent Deo, Sebastien Vievard, Julien Lozi, Marc-Antoine Martinod, Olivier Guyon, Micheal Withford, Simon Gross
Items.Title: Integrated optics beam combiner for the GLINT nulling interferometer
Items.Abstract: The Guided Light Interferometric Nulling Technology (GLINT) instrument operating on the Subaru Telescope in Hawaii uses nulling interferometry as its fundamental operating principle. Nulling interferometry provides an effective way to overcome the contrast and resolution limits of ground-based telescopes by combining the incoming beams so that the starlight is cancelled while the faint signal from an off-axis planet is allowed to pass through. At the heart of GLINT is a newly developed integrated optics beam combiner fabricated in boro-aluminosilicate glass using the femtosecond laser direct-write process. We present the updated design, fabrication and characterisation of this integrated beam combiner which enables simultaneous nulling and fringe tracking in a compact, stable platform suitable for high-contrast astronomical observations.

Items.Authors: Gerard T. van Belle, Jack Moreland
Items.Title: Development work on the MoonLITE Lunar Telescope Array
Items.Abstract: The MoonLITE Engineering Development Unit (EDU) is a laboratory testbed validating key technologies for a lunar, fiber-fed optical interferometer. It focuses on demonstrating stable fiber injection, low-loss beam transport, and robust fringe tracking using a multi-pass delay line and quadrature beam combiner. Early results show strong performance in coupling efficiency, polarization stability, and fringe visibility, confirming the viability of MoonLITE's compact architecture and informing final control, calibration, and error-budget development.

Items.Authors: Jian-Rong Gao, Dingding Ren, J. R. G. Silva, Sofia Cremasco, Z. Zhao, Wenye Ji, Jan de Graaff, Aurèle Adam
Items.Title: Silicon metalens for large terahertz NbN HEB mixer arrays
Items.Abstract: We demonstrate the first use of a silicon-based metalens to couple 1.6 THz radiation to a NbN hot-electron bolometer (HEB). The metalens employs an all-silicon metasurface of subwavelength meta-atoms to realize a Rayleigh–Sommerfeld–derived phase profile, with focusing behavior validated through COMSOL simulations. The metalens-coupled HEB receiver achieves a DSB noise temperature of 1800 K at 1.63 THz and a measured metalens’s power-coupling efficiency of 25%, with a feasible path toward ~80%. Measured far-field beams are Gaussian-like with sidelobes below −14 dB, demonstrating the promise of metalenses for large heterodyne focal-plane arrays. The key results were recently published in D. Ren et al., Appl. Phys. Lett. 127, 202601 (2025), https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0292184.

Items.Authors: Sergio Fabiani, Nicolas De Angelis, Abhay Kumar, Ettore Del Monte, Giovanni Lombardi, on behalf of CUSP Team
Items.Title: The CUbesat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP): mission overview III
Items.Abstract: The CubeSat Solar Polarimeter (CUSP) project, designed to investigate the X-ray linear polarization of solar  flares in the 25–100 keV energy range, is scheduled to conclude Phase B in early July 2026. The mission  comprises an Earth-orbiting CubeSat featuring a Compton scattering polarimeter as its scientific payload.  CUSP will enable the study of magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration within solar flaring magnetic  structures. It is funded by Alcor program of the Italian Space Agency’s (ASI) for new CubeSat missions. We  report on the mission overview following the 19-month Phase B. We developed and tested a polarimeter  prototype to demonstrate the feasibility of this complex detector, which utilizes coincidence measuremen-  ts between plastic scattering bars and GAGG absorber elements. Furthermore, a Structural Model of the  polarimeter core was designed to be tested with vibrations for validating the structural integrity of the bar  retention system under launch conditions.

Items.Authors: Barnaby R. M. Norris, Sergio G. Leon-Saval, Christopher H. Betters, Adam Taras, Yoo Jung Kim, Jonathan Lin, Justin Vella, Jin Wei, Yinzi Xin, Sébastien Vievard, Daniel S. Dahl, Akira Rodziewicz-Ryan, Nathan K. Long, Andrew Ross-Adams, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared Males, Laird M. Close, Nemanja Jovanovic, Vincent Déo, Julien Lozi, Olivier Guyon
Items.Title: The photonic-lantern wavefront sensor and coherent-differential-imager: the next step in full-wave photonic-lantern sensing
Items.Abstract: In recent years the use of the photonic lantern (PL) as a wavefront sensor has seen an explosion of interest, due to its sensitivity to petal and low-wind-effect modes, NCPA resilience, detector efficiency, and spectral resolution. Now, new advances allow the PL to sense far more than just the wavefront: by using an ‘oversampled’ PL (where the number of output fibres exceeds the number of input modes) the complete focal-plane electric field can be measured, including coherence. This enables wavelength-resolved, super-diffraction-limited imaging with speckles removed, essentially ‘undoing’ the seeing. We present the latest on-sky results from the PL wavefront sensor and laboratory results demonstrating the oversampled PL’s coherent-differential-imaging capabilities. We also present details of the multi-headed neural network that enables this, and the development of on-sky instruments designed to exploit this mode including for SCExAO and the Photonic Wavefront Imager (PWI) for MagAO-X.

Items.Authors: Bradley Frank, Younes Chahid, Chris Waring, Amna Waris, Robert Beswick, Louise Chisholm, Chris Pearson
Items.Title: Enabling AI in Astronomy: Platforms and Prototypes Across the UK’s Scientific and Instrumentation Landscape
Items.Abstract: This paper details two UK STFC studies crucial for accelerating AI adoption in astronomy, addressing the complexity of next-generation facilities like SKA.    The first study focused on technical prototypes, resulting in four ML applications for instrumentation: optimized optomechanical design, real-time adaptive optics control, hardware-in-the-loop testing, and novel radio astronomy data processing.    The second study produced a strategic report based on stakeholder engagement and use-case analysis. This report identifies enabling platforms and provides policy guidance, ensuring sustainable AI deployment that adheres to FAIR data requirements.    We present key technical outcomes and critical lessons learned in both software engineering and project management, outlining a necessary roadmap to integrate these ML solutions into robust, production-grade cyberinfrastructure for the UK community.

Items.Authors: Olivier Guyon, Naoshi Murakami, Taro Matsuo, Keigo Enya, Satoshi Itoh, Masayuki Kuzuhara, Jun Nishikawa, Julien Lozi, Sebastien Vievard, Takayuki Kotani, Mona El Morsy, Hajime Kawahara, Manon Lallement, Sandrine Juillard, Jared Males, Michael Bottom, Yoo Jung Kim, Elsa Huby, Nemanja Jovanovic, Michael Fitzgerald, Sylvestre Lacour, Guillermo Martin, Sergio Leon-Saval, Peter Tuthill, Barnaby Norris, Simon Gross, Ruslan Belikov
Items.Title: NIR habitable exoplanet spectroscopy with the matched electric field spectrograph (MEFS)
Items.Abstract: Direct spectroscopy of habitable exoplanets must overcome low source flux and comparatively higher background, requiring exposure times of weeks for the HWO mission. Spectroscopy in the information-rich NIR regime is particularly challenging, as poorer angular resolution exacerbates background mixing, especially near the coronagraph IWA.  We propose to match the post-coronagraph exoplanet electric field to the input of a single-mode spectrograph using a photonic lantern (PL) positioned on the planet location, and feeding a photonic integrated circuit (PIC). We show that the approach offers an order of magnitude gain in exposure time, and extends exoplanet spectroscopy to the NIR regime by enabling a smaller IWA.  We discuss this approach as a NIR spectroscopy module for the HWO mission, and provide an overview of ongoing technology validation activities, including on-sky demonstration of its key elements at the Subaru Telescope.

Items.Authors: Stephen S. Eikenberry, Miguel Bandres, Rodrigo Amezcua-Correa, Miguel Romer, Ameer Batarseh, Tara Crowe, Genevieve Markees, Robert Conwell, David Smith, Daniel Cruz-Delgado, Stephanos Yerolatsitis, Sergio Leon-Saval, Matthew Cooper, Kerri Donaldson-Hanna, Christina Moraitis, Caleb Dobias
Items.Title: Sub-diffraction imaging and precision wavefront sensing with photonic quantum-inspired imaging (PQI2)
Items.Abstract: Photonic lanterns are emerging as a powerful instrument technology for optical and near-infrared modal imaging and wavefront sensing for astronomy applications. Photonic lanterns can provide more general and accurate wavefront sensing performance, as well as sub-diffraction-limited image resolution, when we know the full complex “decoding” transfer matrix between the lantern multimode input end and the single-mode output fiber ports. I will present our group’s recent work on measuring the wavelength-dependent decoding transfer matrices of photonic lanterns, the properties of these matrices, and the resulting phase retrieval performance of the photonic quantum-inspired imaging (PQI2) systems. I will also review recent laboratory and ground-based on-sky test results and potential future applications of PQI2 systems, including as ground-/space-based wavefront sensors, super-resolution imagers, and hybrid focal plane wavefront/science sensors for the Habitable Worlds Observatory.

Items.Authors: D. Scott Acton, N. Schwartz, C. Z. Bond
Items.Title: Petal piston mode measurement for the ELT
Items.Abstract: Measuring the piston errors between the 6 petals of the ELT pupil with a pyramid wavefront sensor (PWFS) presents several challenges. In this paper, we address the problem of accuracy in the piston estimation and robustness in the presence of two-pi ambiguities. We approach this problem by applying a model-based non-linear optimizer to the PWFS output. Simulations show that, even with relatively short integration times, the piston between petals can be robustly and accurately determined, provided a reasonable estimate of RMS of the uncorrected atmospheric turbulence is provided to the optimizer. This technique is also extended to the use of multiple wavelengths to break the 2-pi ambiguity problem, extending the capture range to several microns.

Items.Authors: Jérôme Loicq, Denis Defrère, Romain Laugier, Colin Dandumont, Alexandra Mazzoli, Guilhem Terrassa, Ida Sigusch, Antonin Besse, Rudolf Saathof, Jasper Bouwmeester, Pierre Piron, Imran Khan, Vincent Moreau, Pascal Hallibert, Theresa Rank-Lueftinger, Lucas Schiffano, Luis Venancio, David Alaluf
Items.Title: Exoplanet explorer: single spacecraft nulling interferometer
Items.Abstract: Temperate terrestrial exoplanets are prime targets for the search for extraterrestrial life, but direct atmospheric characterisation in the infrared remains extremely challenging due to high star–planet contrast and small angular separations. Motivated by ESA Voyage 2050 priorities, a consortium funded by ESA and led by TU Delft investigates a dedicated space mission employing a nulling interferometer on a single spacecraft. The study compares architectures using multiple apertures and deployable mechanims (1–3 m diameter, 10–30 m baseline) operating from 3–20 μm, without formation flying, and constrained by Ariane 6 launch capabilities. By combining beams with controlled phase delays, stellar light is suppressed through destructive interference, enabling direct detection of planetary thermal emission. Leveraging recent advances in opto‑mechatronic control, AI-based wavefront stabilization, hyperstable structures, and infrared detectors, the work identifies a very promising concept.

Items.Authors: Malak Galal, Oliver Pineda Suárez, Frédéric Gérôme, Benoît Debord, Fetah Benabid, Jean-Paul Kneib
Items.Title: Comparative study of hollow-core and standard optical fibers for astronomy
Items.Abstract: Efficient light transmission in the blue-visible regime remains a major limitation for fiber-fed astronomical spectrographs, where low photon flux and the intrinsic attenuation of conventional silica fibers reduce survey sensitivity and depth. Inhibited-coupling hollow-core fibers (IC-HCFs) with reduced surface roughness offer a promising alternative, providing guidance predominantly in air and enabling significantly lower loss across the visible spectrum. In this study, we present a comparative evaluation of IC-HCFs against standard multi-mode fibers used in current astronomical instrumentation. We assess the throughput loss that occurs due to bending, twisting, or pinching of the optical fibers when moved using one of the robotic fiber-positioner prototypes designed for next-generation telescopes. These measurements quantify the performance gains offered by IC-HCFs for blue-sensitive spectroscopy and assess their suitability for integration into future survey facilities.

Items.Authors: Andrey M. Baryshev, Jacqueline Hodge, Gie Han Tan, Eva Schinnerer, Stefano Facchini
Items.Title: ALMA2040: the next step in mm/sub-mm radio astronomy
Items.Abstract: In this talk, we present the science case for a next-generation, radically upgraded ALMA-like facility (‘ALMA2040’) based on an European community-driven effort of >400 scientists organized in nine scientific and four technical working groups. We will outline the key scientific drivers that could be uniquely addressed with such a powerful new (sub-)mm interferometer, their synergy with other major astronomical observatories in the 2040’s, and the technical requirements needed to tackle these ambitious goals.  We will present first ideas for a new instrument concept for an ALMA successor. The focus will be on emerging technologies that can enable such an instrument in a cost-effective and sustainable manner.

Items.Authors: Guilhem Terrasa, Jasper Bouwmeester, Felix Wilting, Antonin Besse, Benoit Borguet, Denis Defrère, Colin Dandumont, Imran Khan, Jérôme Loicq, Alexandra Mazzoli, Vincent Moreau, Pierre Piron, Rudolf Saathof, Ida Sigusch, Romain Laugier, Pascal Hallibert, David Alaluf, Theresa Lueftinger, Luca Schifano
Items.Title: Exoplanet explorer: mechanical and thermal design of a single spacecraft nulling interferometer
Items.Abstract: The mechanical and thermal design of a single spacecraft nulling interferometer is presented as part of a new study initiated by the European Space Agency to explore the design parameters and performance of an interferometric concept based on a single spacecraft with multiple sub-apertures. Launch constraints result in strict mass and volume limitations and necessity of secondary mirror deployment. Deployment concepts were evaluated through comparison and modal analysis. Due to thermal considerations, a preliminary thermal model was also developed. Results emphasize the necessity for a multi-layer sunshield and highly reflective materials to achieve the required temperature range. Temperature gradients across the payload and their effects on deformations have been identified as key factors for future investigation. This study provides the first integrated thermo-mechanical concept for the interferometer, laying the groundwork for further analysis and trade-off studies in later phases.

Items.Authors: Andres Parraguez
Items.Title: Prototype of an AI agent for DKIST Science Operations
Items.Abstract: The Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST) is moving out of its Operations Commissioning Phase (OCP). During the OCP (2022-2025), a considerable amount of information was generated to document various aspects of the telescope's operation. Some of this information was captured on Confluence webpages (a wiki system) documenting operational procedures and troubleshooting activities. In addition, Jira was used to report and track technical problems and document workaround procedures when these could be implemented by Science Operations. The DKIST experiments, a structured set of observing programs and metadata, are saved as JSON files. This paper elaborates on the results of a prototype AI agent that uses all available information to answer user questions in operations. The AI agent must have access to all available information, interpret it properly, and provide users with helpful, accurate information to better support operations.

Items.Authors: Shijie Ke, Zhenming Ding, Zeyu Deng, Zhangqi Dang, Jian Ge, Ziyang Zhang
Items.Title: Report on high-performance silica-on-silicon waveguide spectral lens spectrometer
Items.Abstract: An integrated photonic spectrometer based on waveguide spectral lens (WSL) architecture is designed and fabricated on a commercial silica-on-silicon platform. This device integrates the critical functions of spectral dispersion and spatial focusing entirely within planar waveguide arrays, eliminating the need for traditional free-space optical elements like bulk gratings and collimating lenses. With different designs, WSLs can achieve resolving powers ranging from 150 to 21,000 over a broad band from 700 nm to 1600 nm. The fabricated devices also exhibit extremely low polarization dependence and high overall throughput exceeding 60%. The device design and performance test will be reported.

Items.Authors: Peter K. Day, Christopher Albert, Henry LeDuc, Ritoban Basu Thakur, Byeongho Eom, Charles Bradford
Items.Title: Counting far-infrared photons with kinetic inductance detectors
Items.Abstract: We report on far-infrared kinetic inductance detector arrays designed for very low background applications such as spectroscopy with a cold space telescope. We discuss the design and performance of a detector operating at 25 microns, the short wavelength end of the band of interest for a possible far-infrared space mission. The sensitivity of the detectors is enhanced by minimizing the active volume, while efficient optical coupling is maintained with a periodic structure that responds resonantly at the optical frequency. Single 25-micron photons produce high signal to noise pulses in the detector output. We place a limit of a few mHz on the dark count rate. The same detectors are shown to distinguish single photons around 53-microns. We present initial results suggesting that the single-photon sensitivity can be extended to longer wavelength by using the nonlinear response of the detectors to amplify photon signals.

Items.Authors: Abraham D. Falcone, Ian Ashcroft, Michael Betts, William A. Bevidas, Brynn Bortree, David N. Burrows, Zachary Catlin, Joseph Colosimo, Sierra Deppe, Timothy Emeigh, Thomas Forstmeier, Derek Fox, Killian M. Gremling, Md. Arman Hossen, Gavin R. Houlihan, Katie McWhirter, Kadri M. Nizam, Laurel Oneill, David M. Palmer, Abigail A. Raytsis, Lukas R. Stone, Mitchell Wages, Daniel Washington, Michael E. Zugger
Items.Title: The BlackCAT CubeSat: a soft X-ray coded aperture telescope
Items.Abstract: BlackCAT is an X-ray coded-aperture-telescope on a CubeSat, with an early 2026 launch date. It is designed for observations of X-ray sources and transients in the 0.5–20 keV band. The instrument has a wide field of view (0.85 steradian) and is capable of catching gamma ray bursts from the distant universe, galactic transients, flares from blazars, and monitoring the X-ray sky. In addition to the primary high-redshift GRB science, BlackCAT monitors known source variability and searches for rare and exciting new events including gravitational-wave X-ray counterparts, magnetar flares, supernova shock breakouts, and tidal disruption events. The mission functions as a multi-wavelength/messenger complement to present and future facilities, while providing rapid notifications. Silicon X-ray hybrid CMOS detectors form the focal plane array. BlackCAT also serves as a pathfinder for future economical sky monitoring networks. An overview of mission design, science, and status will be presented.

Items.Authors: Boqian Xu, Lingtong Zhang, Lei Jiang, Wei Wang, Meng Zhai, Guohao Ju, Yan Gao, Ye Kuang, Fengyi Jiang, Zhirong Lu, Fei Yan
Items.Title: A 6-m class monolithic aperture UV-Optical Space Telescope Design for Tianlin Habitable Worlds Exploration Mission
Items.Abstract: Surveying nearby stars for the presence of Earth-like planets in the habitable zone has become a key scientific frontier in astronomy. Space planet survey missions will detect thousands of planets, and there will be multiple habitable terrestrial planets among them. To further study these terrestrial planets and to assess whether any Earth-like planets exist in these candidates, analyzing the components of their atmosphere using direct imaging is an effective method, which requires the observatory to deliver high resolution, high contrast, and ultraviolet imaging capabilities. This article will introduce a mission named Tianlin, which was first proposed by NAOC scientists, mainly focusing on characterizing habitable planets around nearby GK type stars. This observatory consists of a 6.6m off-axis monolithic aperture telescope, a coronagraph and other instruments. The working wavelength of the telescope covers down to 200nm, in order to detect the ozone in exoplanet atmospheres.

Items.Authors: Mahmut Eren, Silvia Meakins, Uta Grothkopf, Leslie Kiefer
Items.Title: AI-assisted curation in FUSE: purpose and data-usage classification for the ESO Telescope Bibliography
Items.Abstract: In this talk, we present an AI-assisted extension to FUSE, the ESO Library’s full-text search tool for identifying candidate papers for the ESO Telescope Bibliography (telbib). FUSE finds ESO-related keywords and displays matching passages in context, but keyword matches alone cannot establish whether ESO observational data contributed to scientific results. Two supervised machine-learning models are integrated into the curator interface: the Purpose Model evaluates whether a paper is oriented toward astrophysical discovery, while the Usage Model evaluates whether keyword sentences indicate actual ESO data use. The models support, rather than replace, expert curation. We also compare paper-level decision rules and show that a logistic-regression recommendation layer can improve recall and overall performance while keeping the separate model outputs visible to curators.

Items.Authors: Zhangqi Dang, Jian Ge, Shijie Ke, Zhenming Ding, Ziyang Zhang, Pengjun Zhang, Chaoyan Wang, Jiapeng Zhu, Lingxiao Li
Items.Title: An integrated miniature spectrograph based on waveguide spectral lens
Items.Abstract: We present a transformative approach to astronomical instrumentation: an ultra-compact spectrograph based on waveguide spectral lens (WSL) technology. Addressing the unsustainable growth in size and cost of instruments for future ground- and space-based telescopes, our design leverages integrated photonics to miniaturize spectrographs with different spectral resolution into handheld devices. The core innovation pairs a WSL chip—which simultaneously disperses and focuses light without external optics—with a unique "cylindrical grism lens" for efficient cross-dispersion. Designed for the visible and near-infrared, this instrument interfaces with adaptive optics to enable high-stability, diffraction-limited spectroscopy. This technology promises to revolutionize observational capabilities for astronomy and remote sensing by offering a scalable, cost-effective alternative to traditional giant spectrographs.

Items.Authors: Begoña García-Lorenzo, Julio A. Castro-Almazán, Donaji Esparza-Arredondo, Jose Antonio Acosta-Pulido, Camila de Sá-Freitas, Miska Le Louarn, Ángel Otarola, Jérôme Paufique, Johann Kolb
Items.Title: Diagnosing spatial-coherence outer scale, seeing, and dome-induced turbulence from simultaneous multi-wavelength imaging of point-like sources
Items.Abstract: Atmospheric turbulence causes refractive-index fluctuations that degrade ground-based images. As starlight passes through multiple turbulent layers, the combined effect determines the achievable image quality. Global parameters such as seeing, coherence time, isoplanatic angle, and the wavefront spatial-coherence outer scale (L₀) describe site performance, but L₀ remains poorly constrained, with estimates limited to sparse campaigns.  Turbulence inside telescope enclosures further degrades image quality; although smaller than seeing, dome seeing is still not well characterised, particularly its wavelength dependence.  We present a simple method to estimate L₀ from multi-wavelength point-source imaging in integral-field spectroscopic (IFS) data. The approach also retrieves seeing and dome contributions as a function of wavelength, enabling long-term monitoring. We demonstrate the method with MUSE/VLT data and outline its extension to non-IFS instruments.

Items.Authors: Katherine Elder, Paul Demorest
Items.Title: Testing and validating the next-generation Very Large Array prototype
Items.Abstract: The next-generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) is an astronomical observatory which will operate at centimeter wavelengths (25 to 0.26 centimeters, corresponding to a frequency range of 1.2 GHz to 116 GHz). The observatory will be a synthesis radio telescope consisting of approximately 244 reflector antennas each of 18m diameter. An initial prototype antenna has been constructed and is currently undergoing testing and validation.     We provide an overview of the completed system design of the ngVLA. We also describe the results of the first light observation.

Items.Authors: Ikuyuki Mitsuishi, Yusuke Yoshida, Makoto Yoshihara, Yamato Ishida, Koki Sakuta, Kazuki Ampuku, Ryoma Tanaka, Keitoku Yoshihira, Tetsuo Kano, Naoki Ishida, Yoichi Yatsu, Yoshizumi Miyoshi, Kazushi Asamura, Noriko Yamasaki, Toru Tamagawa, Noriyuki Narukage, Yoshitaka Inoue, Takashi Okajima, Keisuke Tamura, Kikuko Miyata, Philip Kaaret, Gota Yamaguchi, Shutaro Mohri, Takehiro Kume, Yusuke Matsuzawa, Yoichi Imamura, Takahiro Saito, Kentaro Hiraguri, Hirokazu Hashizume, Hidekazu Mimura
Items.Title: Compact, high-sensitivity X-ray imaging spectroscopic instruments for CubeSats: development status, simulations and future prospects
Items.Abstract: We have been developing X-ray optics using our electroforming technique, refined through applications to millimeter-diameter focusing systems used in synchrotron facilities. Single-shell optics fabricated with this method achieved 9 arcsec HPD and a sharp core of <1 arcsec FWHM for FOXSI-5, a sounding rocket experiment for solar flare observations. As a next step, we are developing compact, high-sensitivity imaging spectroscopic instruments with very short-focal-length optics for CubeSat-class missions. Ray-tracing simulations for 6U and 500 mm–class CubeSats with multiple nested mirrors demonstrate expected performance in effective area and angular resolution, while revealing rapid off-axis degradation and strong dependence on mirror size. Vibration tests of a prototype instrument for 500 mm–class CubeSats showed resonance modes below 1000Hz due to mechanical coupling of the mirrors. We summarize recent progress in development and simulations, including scientific feasibility studies.

Items.Authors: Johannes G. Staguhn, Elmer H. Sharp, Ari D. Brown, Felipe A. Colazo Petit, William D. Doriese, Malcolm S. Durkin, Dale J. Fixsen, Suzanne T. Staggs, Kevin L. Denis, Bert G. Harrop, Stephen F. Maher, Vilem Mikula, Edward J. Wollack
Items.Title: Versatile transition edge sensor arrays for FIR space missions
Items.Abstract: We present a new readout architecture for Transition Edge Sensor (TES) based kilopixel arrays with properties that meet the requirements for cryogenic FIR space missions. The 32x16 pixel arrays are connected to time domain SQUID multiplexers by flex lines, so the arrays can be tightly packed. These arrays meet the demanding pixel-density requirements for space missions. The fanout scheme is optimized for using the latest bump-bondable 2D time-domain SQUID multiplexers from NIST, along with a high-density fanout scheme. The noise performance of the detectors is improved by using a modified pixel design over one that our group has meticulously developed and characterized: our new designs include phonon-wavelength sized holes in the legs, meeting background limited requirements for continuum and low- resolution spectroscopy. Moreover, our array design is engineered to be compatible with even lower-noise TES configurations for background-limited medium resolution spectroscopy.

Items.Authors: Ronald Holzlöhner, Michael Esselborn, Xavier Ariño, Henri Bonnet, Martin Brinkmann, Juan-Carlos González-Herrera, Michael Müller, Christophe Vérinaud
Items.Title: Impact of dome seeing in ESO’s ELT on wide-field wavefront correction
Items.Abstract: We are running end-to-end simulations based on transient aerothermal computational fluid dynamics (CFD) of the entire ESO’s ELT telescope, dome and surrounding air volume.    Dome seeing is challenging to AO: spider seeing can drive pupil fragmentation, also known as the petaling effect. Secondly, most of the dome turbulence is optically conjugated to heights between zero and −300 m. Since M4, the telescope deformable mirror (DM), is conjugated to +620 m and secondary DMs are conjugated to even higher altitudes, the WF delivered by the telescope suffers from increasing uncorrectable errors vs. field angle.    The present work refines our previous CFD simulation as follows: We include a) additional open louvers in the dome, b) free convection by adding a buoyancy term to the equations, c) simplified mountain orography model and non-uniform temperature at the dome inlet, d) holes in M1 due to missing segments. We are investigating the WFE at field angles 0–4 arcmin off axis from LGS and NGS.

Items.Authors: Aman Chandra, Hina Suzuki, Heejoo Choi, Adrien Bouskela, Walter Rahmer, Daewook Kim, Christopher Walker, Zac Chen, Changgon Kim
Items.Title: A scalable rigidized inflatable reflector system for next-generation far-infrared space telescopes
Items.Abstract: Inflatable membrane reflectors offer a compelling pathway to realizing large-aperture optical systems for far-infrared and millimeter-wave astronomy. Compared with mechanically deployed reflectors, membrane-based systems provide exceptional advantages in mass efficiency, stowage volume, scalability, and structural simplicity. Our work introduces a novel, instrumentation-driven approach that directly addresses these historical limitations. Central to this approach is an optical architecture that pairs an inflatable primary membrane mirror with precision-machined corrective surfaces, enabling compensation for low-order membrane aberrations and improved far-IR wavefront quality. These innovations are being implemented and validated on a 3-meter prototype reflector, which serves as a critical testbed for understanding inflation behavior, tension-load paths, rigidization performance, and metrology-informed surface correction strategies.

Items.Authors: Ashley Thomas Barnes, Juan Manuel Carmona-Loaiza, Alberto Micol, Martino Romaniello, Stefano Zampieri, Vincenzo Forchì, Diego Rodriguez Mancini, Miguel Vioque, Paula Sánchez-Sáez
Items.Title: Evolving programmatic access to the ESO science archive: from astroquery workflows to natural-language interfaces
Items.Abstract: The ESO Science Archive now supports a richer ecosystem for programmatic access, built around TAP services, the astroquery package, and curated Jupyter notebooks. I will show how recent and planned developments in astroquery.eso and related tools enable common archive tasks — from download-by-programme-ID to multi-mission cross-matching — within a single, reproducible Python environment and a common API shared across multiple observatories. I will also outline an outlook in which natural-language interfaces form a new “bottom rung” of this access ladder, allowing users to ask questions in plain language and obtain concrete datasets and scripts without needing prior experience with ADQL, astroquery, or the Science Archive Portal.

Items.Authors: James P. Gill-Fleming, Meryem K. Dağ, Kieran S. O'Brien
Items.Title: qCMOS single photon counting spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: Modern quantitative CMOS (qCMOS) detectors now achieve sub-electron readout noise, enabling photon-number-resolving performance in compact, room-temperature system without the complexity associated with superconducting or avalanche-photodiode detectors. We demonstrate single-photon counting spectroscopy using the Hamamatsu ORCA-Quest 2, a 4k qCMOS camera (~0.27 e⁻ RMS) integrated with a modest imaging spectrograph (380–750 nm, R≈2300). Per-pixel readout-noise maps and dark-current analysis define the operational limits of large-format qCMOS in the photon-counting regime. Low-flux tests show clear photon-number peak separation and linear spectral response at the single-photon level. These results establish qCMOS as a practical, accessible detector technology for next-generation photon-limited astronomical instruments.

Items.Authors: André J. van Es, Mark Waterson, Robert Haigh, Ivan Lloro, Randall Wayth, Lucio Tirone, Luca Stringhetti, Robert Laing, Alan Davis, Raunaq Bhushan, Pieter Benthem, Marco Caiazzo, Giulia Macario, Shinichiro Asayama, Jess Broderick, Maria Grazia Labate, Danny Price, Maciej Serylak, Riley Keel, Charlotte Sobey, Jimi Green, Ravi Subrahmanyan, Bartosz Idzkowski, Jader Monari, Gianni Bernardi, Pietro Bolli, Carolina Belli, Letizia Caito, Simone Chiarucci, Giovanni Comoretto, Paola Di Ninni, Andrea Mattana, Federico Perini, Giuseppe Pupillo, Marco Schiaffino, Monica Alderighi, Carlo Baffa, Sergio D'Angelo, Davide Fierro, Elisabeth Giani, Giovanni Naldi, Marco Poloni, Simone Rusticelli, Francesco Schiliro, Federica Caputo, Tom Booler, David Davidson, Dave Minchin, Andy McPhail, Maria Kovaleva, Marcin Sokolowski, Jishnu N. Thekkeppattu, Steven Tingay, Daniel Ung, Angela Teale, Kris Zarb Adami, Raphael Thenevin, Aniket Hendre, Jan Geralt Bij de Vaate, Riccardo Chiello, Marchel Gerbers, Jacopo Nanni, Peter Hall, Alessio Magro, Robert Braun, Giovanni Tartarini, Giuseppe Virone, Georgios Kyriakou
Items.Title: The road to SKA-Low from a station prototype to a system prototype: the journey to SKA-Low AA0.5
Items.Abstract: This presentation presents a comprehensive overview of the prototyping and verification activities that laid the foundation for the construction of the SKA-Low telescope. It traces the evolution from early experimental platforms (AAVS0--3) culminating in the deployment of the first four fully integrated SKA-Low stations (AA0.5). These stations, delivered as part of the AA0.5 milestone, bring together all essential subsystems of the telescope — from antennas and digitisation to signal processing and control — demonstrating end-to-end functionality at scale. The paper highlights key technical achievements, lessons learned, and the critical role of prototyping in de-risking design decisions ahead of full array construction.

Items.Authors: Zi-hang Zhu, Ze-yu Zhu, Zhi-hao Cao, Feng Li, Jian Wang
Items.Title: WFST-ChatOps: a domain-adapted qa chatbot for the wide field survey telescope
Items.Abstract: Artificial intelligence and large language models are reshaping how humans access knowledge, collaborate on complex projects, and support critical operations. For large scientific facilities, AI assistants can help operators understand system design and obtain guidance during routine procedures and incidents.The Mozi Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST) is a wide-field time-domain survey facility with a sophisticated hardware–software stack, creating a strong need for tools that support observation operations with reliable domain knowledge. In this work we construct a specialized question–answer dataset covering scenario-based queries on project explanations and day-to-day operations, and we use DeepSeek-R1-32B model via parameter-efficient fine-tuning to obtain WFST-ChatOps（Chat-Operations）, a domain-oriented QA chatbot that provides natural-language access to WFST project information, design reports, and operation manuals.

Items.Authors: David Murphy, Vincent Tatischeff, Philippe Laurent, Mark Pearce, Lorraine Hanlon, Aline Meuris, Prerna Baranwal, Christophe Beigbeder, Derek Bennet, Charles Boreux, Arnaud Claret, Nicolas de Séréville, Nicolas Dosme, Eric Doumayrou, Nathan Franel, Mariya Georgieva, Sally Hankache, Jimmy Jeglot, Mózsi Kiss, Beng-Yun Ky, Vincent Lafage, Christine Le Galliard, Joseph Mangan, Caimin McKenna, Jean Peyré, Arjun Poitaya, Marin Prieur, Diana Renaud, Arnaud Saussac, Aman Shetty, Alexey Uliyanov, Colin Wade, Phil Webster, Varun Varun, Camille Pirat
Items.Title: COMCUBE-S: a CubeSat swarm for GRB polarimetry and localisation
Items.Abstract: COMCUBE-S is a proposed CubeSat swarm mission designed to provide polarisation measurements of Gamma-Ray Burst prompt emission as well as all-sky monitoring for high-energy time domain astronomy, with rapid alert notifications in response to high energy transients.    The mission consists of 28 16U CubeSats. Each satellite carries an advanced miniaturised Compton telescope allowing COMCUBE-S to make temporal, spectral, and polarimetric measurements of gamma-rays in the tens of keV to a few MeV range    The swarm satellites will be equally distributed along an equatorial orbit, forming a closed ring of intersatellite links. Satellites in the swarm are able to identify high-energy transients, relay data to the ground and distribute source locations to observatories worldwide for follow-up. COMCUBE-S will localise 160 GRBs per year with positions distributed within 120 s.    The project has completed a Phase A study with ESA and aims to launch a two-satellite in-orbit demonstarion by 2030.

Items.Authors: Miska Le Louarn, J. A. Castro-Almazán, D. Esparza-Arredondo, M. B. García-Lorenzo, J. A. Acosta-Pulido, J. Kolb, A. Otarola, J. Paufique, C. de Sa Freitas
Items.Title: Comparing turbulence outer scale measurements on-sky between LGS-WFS data and MUSE image-cubes at the VLT
Items.Abstract: The Outer scale of turbulence (L0) will play a significant role in the performance of Adaptive Optics (AO) instruments at the ELT, especially those based on laser guide stars (LGS), through the distribution of turbulent power in the low order modes. It is therefore important to understand this parameter. In this contribution, we present results from a measurement campaign at the Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal Observatory to measure simultaneously the outer scale through two independent methods. The first method is based on LGS wavefront sensor measurements, using the AO facility (AOF). The second method relies on the variation of image quality (IQ) with wavelength at the focal plane of the MUSE Integral Field Spectrograph (IFS) in its Wide Field Mode (MUSE-WFM). We compare the L0 values obtained through the two methods, using different AO modes. With weak Tip-Tilt (TT) correction we find a good correlation between the two methods, giving confidence in their accuracy.

Items.Authors: Kenichi Karatsu, Shahab Dabironezare, Louis Marting, Leon Olde Scholtenhuis, Daniela Perez Capelo, David Thoen, Alejandro Pascual Laguna, Sten Vollebregt, Akira Endo, Jochem Baselmans
Items.Title: Development of broadband spectro-polarimetric arrays for next-generation CMB observations
Items.Abstract: A new spectro-polarimeter array has been developed for next-generation Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) instruments. The design features 14 spatial pixels, each consisting of a polarization-separating broadband leaky-wave lens-antenna, with each single-polarization output connected to a high-sensitivity, low-resolution 22-channel mm/sub-mm on-chip filterbank operating in a frequency range from 135–270 GHz. The device uses kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) to detect the power in each spectral band. The array with ~600 KIDs was fabricated and measured, demonstrating a cross-polarization level lower than –15 dB and an averaged filter peak efficiency of 67%. The design is compact and scalable towards larger arrays. The results show promise for achieving a large-format spectro-polarimetric focal plane array for future CMB instruments.

Items.Authors: Felix A. Dannert, Philipp A. Huber, Romain Laugier, Thomas Birbacher, Jonah T. Hansen, Adrian M. Glauser, Quanz P. Sascha
Items.Title: The impact of instrumental perturbations on exoplanet yields for the LIFE Space Mission
Items.Abstract: Exoplanet yield estimates used to assess the scientific return of future high-contrast imaging missions systematically underestimate mission risks, because they do not explicitly include instrumental systematics. For the first time, and in the context of the Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE), we quantify how instrument perturbations propagate into the yield estimates, which allows us to put robust requirements on instrument stability. Beyond nulling interferometry, this framework could offer a pathway towards addressing similar open questions for future single aperture telescopes, where stability is known to play an equally important role.

Items.Authors: Leanne P. Guy, Connor Yablonski, Aaron M. Meisner, Guillem Megias Homar, Merlin Fisher-Levine, Eman E. Ali, Tiger J. Hu, Christopher W. Stubbs
Items.Title: Development of a retrieval-augmented generation chatbot for enhanced information discovery at Rubin Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s LSST will produce petabytes of data supported by a large, heterogeneous set of technical documents, operational guides, and scientific notes. Because this material is distributed across numerous platforms and formats, including internal systems, users and general-purpose language models often find it difficult to locate reliable Rubin-specific information. To address this, we developed a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) virtual assistant that provides context-aware, factual access to Rubin’s documentation ecosystem. The system aggregates content from multiple sources and performs semantic search through a conversational interface, using Weaviate for embeddings, LangChain for query orchestration, and an OpenAI GPT model as the LLM backend. Grounding responses in domain-specific knowledge reduces hallucinations, improves accuracy, and demonstrates the potential of RAG to streamline workflows and support effective use of LSST data products.

Items.Authors: Nuwanthika Fernando, Brent Miszalski, Nuria Lorente, Anthony Horton
Items.Title: MAVIS- Final design of the data reduction pipeline
Items.Abstract: MAVIS is the MCAO Assisted Visible Imager and Spectrograph, the first MCAO-facility instrument planned for the VLT which will provide a near diffraction-limited view of the visible wavelength. We present the final design for the Data Reduction Pipeline of the instrument, and describe the prototyping for the design of calibration methods and dataflows. For the spectrograph calibrations, the geometry of the slices is determined using a series of moving pinhole mask exposures. Prototyping the geometry recipe resulted in the change to the pinhole mask design. This also confirmed the need for etalons for the wavelength calibration, to achieve required accuracies in the low resolution blue mode. Early prototyping of the DRS has been beneficial to the design of the entire instrument. The critical algorithms used ESO’s PyCPL libraries, the GNU Scientific Library, and data workflows at each stage were drafted using the new EDPS (ESO Data Processing System) libraries.

Items.Authors: S. Perez, M. Bonati, B. Cervantes, A. Lapi, A. Varela, E. Schiller, A. Drlica-Wagner, G. Damke, C. Chavez, J. Estrada, G. Pinaroli, G. Fernandez-Moroni, M. Makler, J. Tiffenberg
Items.Title: SkipperCam: a wide-field skipper-CCD pathfinder for high-cadence imaging with sub-electron capabilities
Items.Abstract: We present SkipperCam, a Skipper-CCD imager pathfinder demonstrating low-noise, high-cadence wide-field imaging. It deploys a 20-sensor Skipper-CCD focal plane (~27 Mpix) on the 0.6 m Curtis–Schmidt telescope at CTIO, reusing the PreCam camera body, shutter, and filter wheel. A massively parallel, MIDNA-based readout decouples the usual trade-off between low noise and slow readout, delivering a ~2 deg² field of view with ~2 s full-frame cadence and ~7 e⁻ noise in fast survey mode, while reaching sub-electron noise via multiple non-destructive sampling. Primarily a technology demonstrator, it is also optimized for early science through a high-cadence microlensing survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud targeting short-timescale events from low-mass compact objects, with opportunities in photometric variability, transient detection, blue-sensitive imaging, and stellar-occultation follow-ups. SkipperCam is the first on-sky demonstration of a multiplexed Skipper-CCD array in survey mode.
